CHAPTER 11 - SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION

Introduction

Look around and you will find motions that repeat: the swing of a pendulum, the vibration of a guitar string, the bobbing of a mass on a spring, the beating of the heart, and the alternating current in a wire. All of these are examples of periodic motion. Among periodic motions, the simplest and most important is simple harmonic motion (SHM). It is important not only because it describes many natural oscillations directly, but also because any complicated periodic motion can be built up from simple harmonic motions. This chapter develops the mathematics and physics of SHM from first principles and applies it to the simple pendulum, the loaded spring, and to damped and forced oscillations.

11.1 PERIODIC AND OSCILLATORY MOTION

A motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time is called periodic motion. The interval after which the motion repeats is the time period. The revolution of a planet around the Sun and the motion of the hands of a clock are periodic. A special class of periodic motion is oscillatory (or vibratory) motion, in which a body moves to and fro repeatedly about a fixed mean (equilibrium) position. A swinging pendulum and a vibrating spring are oscillatory. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory - uniform circular motion is periodic yet not to and fro.

11.2 SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION

An oscillatory motion is said to be simple harmonic if the restoring force acting on the body is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards that mean position. In symbols,
   F = -k x,
where x is the displacement, k is the force constant, and the negative sign shows that the force opposes the displacement (it always pushes or pulls the body back towards the centre). Using Newton's second law F = m a, we get m a = -k x, so
   a = -(k/m) x = -omega^2 x,   where omega^2 = k/m.
The quantity omega is called the angular frequency. The relation a = -omega^2 x is the defining equation of SHM: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed oppositely. Any system whose acceleration obeys this relation executes SHM.

11.3 DISPLACEMENT, VELOCITY AND ACCELERATION

The solution of a = -omega^2 x is a sinusoidal function of time. The displacement of a particle in SHM can be written as
   x = A sin(omega t + phi).
Here A is the amplitude (the maximum displacement from the mean position), (omega t + phi) is the phase, and phi is the initial phase or epoch, which fixes the state of the particle at t = 0.
Differentiating with respect to time gives the velocity:
   v = dx/dt = A omega cos(omega t + phi).
Using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, we can write the velocity in terms of position:
   v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
The velocity is maximum, v_max = A omega, at the mean position (x = 0), and zero at the extreme positions (x = A). Differentiating again gives the acceleration:
   a = dv/dt = -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x.
The acceleration is zero at the mean position and maximum in magnitude, a_max = A omega^2, at the extremes, always pointing back towards the centre. Notice the phase relationships: the velocity leads the displacement by pi/2, and the acceleration is exactly out of phase (by pi) with the displacement.

11.4 TIME PERIOD, FREQUENCY AND PHASE

The particle returns to the same state when the phase increases by 2 pi. Therefore the time period, the time for one complete oscillation, is
   T = 2 pi / omega.
The frequency f is the number of oscillations per second,
   f = 1/T = omega / (2 pi),   and so   omega = 2 pi f.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz); angular frequency omega in radian per second. The phase (omega t + phi) tells us the position and direction of motion of the particle at any instant. Two particles are said to be in phase if their phase difference is zero (or a whole multiple of 2 pi) and in opposite phase if the difference is pi. A phase difference of pi/2 means one quantity is a quarter cycle ahead of the other, as the velocity is ahead of the displacement.

Worked example 1. A body moving in SHM has a = -64 x (SI units). Find omega and T. Comparing with a = -omega^2 x, omega^2 = 64, so omega = 8 rad/s and T = 2 pi / 8 = 0.785 s.

11.5 ENERGY IN SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION

A particle in SHM continually exchanges kinetic and potential energy while their sum stays constant. With v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2), the kinetic energy is
   KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2).
The restoring force is F = -m omega^2 x, so the work done against it in moving from the mean position to displacement x is stored as potential energy,
   PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2.
Adding the two, the total mechanical energy is
   E = KE + PE = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.
This is independent of x and t, confirming conservation of energy. The total energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude and to the square of the angular frequency. At the mean position all the energy is kinetic; at the extremes it is all potential. The kinetic and potential energies are equal at x = A/sqrt(2), each being half of the total. Because KE and PE vary as sin^2 and cos^2, they oscillate at twice the frequency of the displacement.

Worked example 2. A particle of mass 2 kg executes SHM with A = 0.1 m and omega = 10 rad/s. Then E = (1/2)(2)(10^2)(0.1^2) = 1 J; v_max = A omega = 1 m/s; a_max = A omega^2 = 10 m/s^2. At x = 0.05 m, KE = (1/2)(2)(100)(0.01 - 0.0025) = 0.75 J and PE = 0.25 J.

11.6 THE REFERENCE CIRCLE

SHM can be visualised as the projection of uniform circular motion. Imagine a particle P moving with constant angular speed omega on a circle of radius A. At time t its angular position is (omega t + phi). The foot of the perpendicular from P onto a diameter moves back and forth executing SHM with displacement x = A sin(omega t + phi). The centripetal acceleration A omega^2 of P, projected onto the diameter, gives -omega^2 x, exactly the SHM acceleration. The reference circle thus explains why the period of SHM is T = 2 pi / omega, the same as the time for one revolution.

11.7 THE SIMPLE PENDULUM

A simple pendulum is an idealised bob of mass m on a light, inextensible string of length L. When displaced through a small angle theta, the restoring force is the tangential component of gravity, F = -mg sin theta. For small angles sin theta is approximately theta, and the arc displacement is x = L theta, so
   F = -mg theta = -(mg/L) x.
Comparing with F = -k x, the force constant is k = mg/L, giving omega = sqrt(g/L) and
   T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
The period depends only on the length and on g; it is independent of the mass of the bob and of the amplitude, provided the amplitude is small. A seconds pendulum, which takes one second for each swing (T = 2 s), has length L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2), about 0.99 m at g = 9.8 m/s^2.

Worked example 3. A pendulum of length 1.0 m at g = 9.8 m/s^2 has T = 2 pi sqrt(1/9.8) = 2.0 s.

11.8 THE LOADED SPRING

When a mass m hangs from a spring of force constant k and is displaced by x, Hooke's law gives the restoring force F = -k x. Newton's second law then yields a = -(k/m) x, so the motion is SHM with
   omega = sqrt(k/m)   and   T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
The stiffer the spring (larger k) or the smaller the mass, the faster the oscillation.
Springs in parallel: when two springs of constants k1 and k2 support the same mass and share the same displacement, their forces add, so the effective constant is k = k1 + k2. The combination is stiffer, so the period is shorter.
Springs in series: when the springs are joined end to end, the same force stretches both and their extensions add, so 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2, giving k = k1 k2/(k1 + k2). The combination is softer, so the period is longer.

Worked example 4. A 0.2 kg mass on a spring of k = 80 N/m has T = 2 pi sqrt(0.2/80) = 2 pi (0.05) = 0.314 s and f = 1/T = 3.18 Hz.

11.9 FREE, DAMPED AND FORCED OSCILLATIONS; RESONANCE

Free oscillations occur when a body is displaced and released; it then oscillates at its own natural frequency f0, set by its inertia and stiffness, with (ideally) constant amplitude. In practice, friction, air resistance and internal losses continuously remove energy, so the amplitude decreases with time; such oscillations are called damped oscillations. The heavier the damping, the faster the decay. If a periodic external force of frequency f is applied to keep the body oscillating, the motion is a forced oscillation, and the body oscillates at the driving frequency f rather than at its own natural frequency.
When the driving frequency is made equal to the natural frequency (f = f0), energy is transferred to the system most efficiently and the amplitude grows very large. This condition is called resonance. Resonance can be useful - tuning a radio adjusts a circuit's natural frequency to match a station's frequency, strongly amplifying that signal. It can also be dangerous - marching soldiers break step on a bridge so that their footfall frequency does not match the bridge's natural frequency and set it into destructive resonance.

SUMMARY

- Periodic motion repeats after equal time intervals; oscillatory motion is periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
- SHM is defined by F = -k x, equivalently a = -omega^2 x, with omega = sqrt(k/m).
- Displacement x = A sin(omega t + phi); velocity v = A omega cos(omega t + phi) = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2); acceleration a = -omega^2 x.
- v_max = A omega at the mean position; a_max = A omega^2 at the extremes.
- Time period T = 2 pi / omega; frequency f = 1/T = omega/(2 pi); omega = 2 pi f.
- Energy: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, total E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 (constant, proportional to A^2).
- SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter (reference circle).
- Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), independent of mass and amplitude (small swings).
- Loaded spring: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); parallel springs k = k1 + k2 (shorter T), series springs 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2 (longer T).
- Free oscillation at natural frequency; damped oscillation loses amplitude; forced oscillation driven externally; resonance occurs when driving frequency equals natural frequency.

chapter_summary.title: Simple Harmonic Motion - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This summary of NIOS Senior Secondary Physics Chapter 11 develops simple harmonic motion from the restoring-force condition F = -k x. It covers displacement, velocity, acceleration, time period, frequency, phase, energy, the reference circle, the simple pendulum and loaded spring, and damped, forced and resonant oscillations.

Parallel springs add their constants (shorter period); series springs add reciprocals (longer period).

glossary.definition: A motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time, such as a planet orbiting the Sun.
Periodic to-and-fro motion of a body about a fixed mean (equilibrium) position.
Oscillatory motion in which the restoring force is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position, F = -k x.
The maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position in an oscillation, denoted A.
The rate of change of phase, omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f, related to the force constant by omega = sqrt(k/m).
The time taken to complete one full oscillation, T = 2 pi / omega.
The number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T, measured in hertz.
The quantity (omega t + phi) that specifies the position and direction of motion of a particle at a given instant.
The force that acts to bring an oscillating body back to its mean position, F = -k x in SHM.
An idealised point mass on a light inextensible string; its period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) for small swings.
A pendulum whose time period is 2 s (one second per swing); its length is about 0.99 m at g = 9.8 m/s^2.
The force per unit extension of a spring, k, appearing in Hooke's law F = -k x and in T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
An oscillation whose amplitude decreases with time because resistive forces remove energy.
An oscillation maintained by a periodic external force, occurring at the driving frequency.
The large-amplitude response of a system when the driving frequency equals its natural frequency.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Simple Harmonic Motion (NIOS Class 12 Physics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show your working for numerical problems. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2 and pi^2 = 9.87 where required. Use plain notation (omega, sqrt, pi).

questions.question: Define simple harmonic motion and state the two equivalent conditions it must satisfy.
questions.answer: SHM is oscillatory motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and directed towards it. The conditions are F = -k x and, equivalently, a = -omega^2 x, where omega = sqrt(k/m) and the minus sign shows the force opposes the displacement.
questions.explanation: State F = -k x and a = -omega^2 x.

questions.question: Calculate the time period of a simple pendulum of length 1.0 m at a place where g = 9.8 m/s^2.
questions.answer: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 pi sqrt(1.0/9.8) = 2 pi sqrt(0.102) = 2 pi x 0.319 = 2.0 s (approximately).
questions.explanation: Substitute L = 1.0 m and g = 9.8 in T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

questions.question: A mass of 0.2 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 80 N/m. Find its time period and frequency of oscillation.
questions.answer: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) = 2 pi sqrt(0.2/80) = 2 pi sqrt(0.0025) = 2 pi x 0.05 = 0.314 s. Frequency f = 1/T = 1/0.314 = 3.18 Hz.
questions.explanation: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); f = 1/T.

questions.question: A particle of mass 2 kg executes SHM with amplitude 0.1 m and angular frequency 10 rad/s. Find its total energy, maximum velocity and maximum acceleration.
questions.answer: Total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = 0.5 x 2 x 100 x 0.01 = 1 J. Maximum velocity v_max = A omega = 0.1 x 10 = 1 m/s. Maximum acceleration a_max = A omega^2 = 0.1 x 100 = 10 m/s^2.
questions.explanation: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2; v_max = A omega; a_max = A omega^2.

questions.question: Starting from x = A sin(omega t + phi), derive the expressions for velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM. Show that v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) and a = -omega^2 x, and state where velocity and acceleration are maximum.
questions.answer: Displacement: x = A sin(omega t + phi). Velocity v = dx/dt = A omega cos(omega t + phi). Using cos = sqrt(1 - sin^2), v = A omega sqrt(1 - x^2/A^2) = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). Acceleration a = dv/dt = -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x. Velocity is maximum (A omega) at the mean position (x = 0) and zero at the extremes; acceleration is maximum (A omega^2) at the extremes and zero at the mean position.
questions.explanation: Differentiate twice and use the trig identity.

questions.question: What is meant by the phase of a particle in SHM, and what does a phase difference of pi indicate?
questions.answer: The phase is the quantity (omega t + phi) in x = A sin(omega t + phi); it specifies the position and direction of motion of the particle at an instant. A phase difference of pi between two particles means they are exactly out of step: when one is at its positive extreme the other is at its negative extreme.
questions.explanation: Phase is the argument of the sine; pi means opposite phase.

questions.question: Find the length of a seconds pendulum (time period 2 s) at a place where g = 9.8 m/s^2 (take pi^2 = 9.87).
questions.explanation: Rearrange T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) to L = g T^2/(4 pi^2).

questions.question: Derive expressions for the kinetic, potential and total energy of a particle in SHM and show that the total energy is constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude.
questions.answer: With v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2), KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2). The restoring force is F = -m omega^2 x, so PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2. Total energy E = KE + PE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) + (1/2) m omega^2 x^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2. This has no x or t, so it is constant, and it is proportional to A^2. KE is maximum at the mean position and PE at the extremes; they are equal at x = A/sqrt(2).
questions.explanation: Add KE and PE; the x-terms cancel to give (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.

questions.question: Distinguish between free, damped and forced oscillations, and state the condition for resonance.
questions.answer: Free oscillations occur at a body's natural frequency after it is displaced and released, with constant amplitude (ideal case). Damped oscillations lose amplitude with time because resistive forces remove energy. Forced oscillations are driven by a periodic external force and occur at the driving frequency. Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, producing a very large amplitude.
questions.explanation: Free = natural frequency; damped = decaying; forced = driven; resonance at f = f0.

questions.question: Two springs each of force constant 100 N/m are connected to the same mass, first in parallel and then in series. Find the effective spring constant in each case and state which gives the shorter time period.
questions.answer: Parallel: k = k1 + k2 = 100 + 100 = 200 N/m. Series: 1/k = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so k = 50 N/m. Since T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), a larger k gives a shorter period, so the parallel combination (200 N/m) gives the shorter period.
questions.explanation: Parallel adds k; series adds 1/k; larger k means shorter T.

questions.question: Define simple harmonic motion and state the condition it must satisfy.
questions.answer: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is the to-and-fro oscillatory motion of a particle in which the restoring force acting on it is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards that mean position. The defining condition is F = -k x, or equivalently a = -omega^2 x, where the negative sign shows the force (and acceleration) opposes the displacement.
questions.explanation: State F = -k x and a = -omega^2 x.

questions.question: Distinguish between periodic motion and oscillatory (vibratory) motion.
questions.answer: Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time (for example, the motion of the hands of a clock or a planet around the Sun). Oscillatory motion is a special kind of periodic motion in which a body moves to and fro about a fixed mean position (for example, a pendulum or a vibrating spring). Thus every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory.
questions.explanation: Oscillatory is a subset of periodic (to-and-fro about a mean position).

questions.question: A particle moves such that its acceleration is a = -16 x (SI units). Show that this is SHM and find its time period.
questions.answer: Comparing a = -16 x with the SHM condition a = -omega^2 x, we identify omega^2 = 16, so omega = 4 rad/s. Because the acceleration is proportional to displacement and oppositely directed, the motion is SHM. The time period is T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 4 = pi/2 = 1.57 s.
questions.explanation: Match to a = -omega^2 x; omega = 4, T = pi/2 s.

questions.question: Write the equation for displacement in SHM and name each symbol.
questions.answer: The displacement is x = A sin(omega t + phi). Here x is the displacement from the mean position at time t, A is the amplitude (maximum displacement), omega is the angular frequency, t is the time, and phi is the initial phase (epoch) which fixes the position of the particle at t = 0.
questions.explanation: Name x, A, omega, t, phi.

questions.question: Starting from x = A sin(omega t), obtain expressions for velocity and acceleration and state where each is maximum.
questions.answer: Velocity v = dx/dt = A omega cos(omega t). Acceleration a = dv/dt = -A omega^2 sin(omega t) = -omega^2 x. The velocity is maximum (v_max = A omega) at the mean position (x = 0, where cos = 1) and zero at the extremes. The acceleration is maximum in magnitude (a_max = A omega^2) at the extreme positions (x = A) and zero at the mean position.
questions.explanation: Differentiate twice; v_max at mean, a_max at extremes.

questions.question: Show that in SHM the velocity at displacement x is v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
questions.answer: From x = A sin(omega t + phi), v = A omega cos(omega t + phi). Using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, cos(omega t + phi) = sqrt(1 - (x/A)^2). Therefore v = A omega sqrt(1 - x^2/A^2) = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2). At x = 0, v = A omega (maximum); at x = A, v = 0.
questions.explanation: Use the trig identity to eliminate time.

questions.question: A particle in SHM has amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad/s. Find its maximum velocity and maximum acceleration.
questions.answer: Maximum velocity v_max = A omega = 0.05 x 20 = 1.0 m/s. Maximum acceleration a_max = A omega^2 = 0.05 x 20^2 = 0.05 x 400 = 20 m/s^2.
questions.explanation: v_max = A omega, a_max = A omega^2.

questions.question: A SHM particle of amplitude 10 cm has speed 8 cm/s when its displacement is 6 cm. Find its angular frequency and time period.
questions.answer: Using v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2): 8 = omega sqrt(10^2 - 6^2) = omega sqrt(100 - 36) = omega x 8. Hence omega = 1 rad/s. Time period T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi = 6.28 s.
questions.explanation: Solve v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) for omega, then T.

questions.question: The displacement of a particle is x = 0.02 sin(50 t) m. Find its amplitude, angular frequency and maximum speed.
questions.answer: Comparing with x = A sin(omega t): amplitude A = 0.02 m, angular frequency omega = 50 rad/s. Maximum speed v_max = A omega = 0.02 x 50 = 1.0 m/s.
questions.explanation: Read A and omega from the equation; v_max = A omega.

questions.question: Define time period, frequency and angular frequency of SHM and give the relations between them.
questions.answer: Time period T is the time taken to complete one full oscillation. Frequency f is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T, measured in hertz. Angular frequency omega measures the rate of phase change, omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f. Thus T = 2 pi / omega and f = omega / (2 pi).
questions.explanation: T = 1/f = 2 pi / omega; omega = 2 pi f.

questions.question: What is meant by the phase of a particle in SHM? What is a phase difference of pi?
questions.answer: The phase of a particle in SHM x = A sin(omega t + phi) is the quantity (omega t + phi); it specifies the state (position and direction of motion) of the particle at a given instant. A phase difference of pi radians between two particles means they are exactly out of step: when one is at its positive extreme the other is at its negative extreme, and they always move in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Phase = argument of sine; pi = opposite phase.

questions.question: A body executing SHM completes 30 oscillations in one minute. Find its frequency, time period and angular frequency.
questions.answer: Frequency f = 30 oscillations / 60 s = 0.5 Hz. Time period T = 1/f = 2 s. Angular frequency omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 0.5 = pi = 3.14 rad/s.
questions.explanation: f = N/t, T = 1/f, omega = 2 pi f.

questions.question: A particle of mass 0.2 kg executes SHM of amplitude 0.1 m and angular frequency 10 rad/s. Find its total energy and its kinetic energy at x = 0.06 m.
questions.explanation: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2; KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2).

questions.question: Show that in SHM the kinetic and potential energies are equal at x = A/sqrt(2).
questions.answer: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) and PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2. Setting KE = PE gives A^2 - x^2 = x^2, so 2 x^2 = A^2 and x = A/sqrt(2). At this displacement each equals half the total energy (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.
questions.explanation: Set the two expressions equal and solve.

questions.question: Sketch in words how KE and PE vary with position in SHM and state where each is maximum.
questions.answer: As the particle moves from the mean position to an extreme, its kinetic energy falls from a maximum (at x = 0) to zero (at x = A), while its potential energy rises from zero (at x = 0) to a maximum (at x = A). At every point KE + PE equals the constant total energy (1/2) m omega^2 A^2. KE is maximum at the mean position; PE is maximum at the extremes.
questions.explanation: KE max at mean, PE max at extremes, sum constant.

questions.question: Calculate the length of a simple pendulum whose time period is 2 s (g = 9.8 m/s^2).
questions.answer: From T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), squaring gives T^2 = 4 pi^2 L / g, so L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). Substituting: L = 9.8 x 4 / (4 x 9.87) = 39.2 / 39.48 = 0.993 m, about 0.99 m. This is the length of a seconds pendulum.

questions.question: A mass of 0.5 kg attached to a spring oscillates with a period of 0.5 s. Find the spring constant.
questions.answer: From T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), T^2 = 4 pi^2 m / k, so k = 4 pi^2 m / T^2. Substituting: k = 4 x 9.87 x 0.5 / 0.25 = 19.74 / 0.25 = 78.96 N/m, about 79 N/m.

questions.question: State two factors on which the period of a simple pendulum depends and two on which it does not.
questions.answer: The period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) depends on (i) the length L of the pendulum and (ii) the acceleration due to gravity g at the place. It does NOT depend on (i) the mass of the bob or (ii) the amplitude of swing, provided the amplitude is small (angle less than about 4 degrees).
questions.explanation: Depends on L and g; independent of mass and (small) amplitude.

questions.question: Two springs of constants k1 and k2 are connected (a) in parallel and (b) in series to the same mass. Find the effective spring constant in each case and state which gives the shorter period.
questions.answer: (a) Parallel: both springs share the same displacement and their forces add, so k_parallel = k1 + k2 (stiffer). (b) Series: the same force acts through both and their extensions add, so 1/k_series = 1/k1 + 1/k2, giving k_series = k1 k2/(k1 + k2) (softer). Since T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), a larger k gives a shorter period. Therefore the parallel combination gives the shorter period.
questions.explanation: Parallel adds k; series adds 1/k; larger k = shorter T.

questions.question: Two identical springs each of constant 120 N/m are joined in series and then in parallel. Find the effective constant in each case.
questions.answer: Series: 1/k = 1/120 + 1/120 = 2/120, so k = 60 N/m. Parallel: k = 120 + 120 = 240 N/m. The series combination is softer (60 N/m) and the parallel combination is stiffer (240 N/m).
questions.explanation: Series 60 N/m; parallel 240 N/m.

questions.question: Distinguish between free, damped and forced oscillations.
questions.answer: Free oscillations occur when a body is displaced and released, oscillating at its own natural frequency with constant amplitude (in the ideal, friction-free case). Damped oscillations are oscillations whose amplitude gradually decreases with time because friction or resistive forces continuously remove energy. Forced oscillations are oscillations maintained by a periodic external driving force; the body then oscillates at the driving frequency rather than its own natural frequency.
questions.explanation: Free: natural frequency; damped: decaying amplitude; forced: driven.

questions.question: What is resonance? Give one everyday example and explain why it can be dangerous.
questions.answer: Resonance is the condition in forced oscillations in which the frequency of the external driving force equals the natural frequency of the system, causing the amplitude of oscillation to become very large. An everyday example is pushing a swing at just the right rhythm so it goes higher and higher. It can be dangerous because the very large amplitude may cause structures to fail; for instance, soldiers break step while crossing a bridge so their marching frequency does not match the bridge's natural frequency and set it into destructive resonance.
questions.explanation: Driving frequency = natural frequency; large amplitude; bridge example.

questions.question: Explain periodic and oscillatory motion, define SHM, and show that a body obeying F = -k x executes SHM. Derive the expression for its angular frequency.
questions.answer:
Periodic motion is any motion that repeats after equal time intervals (a planet orbiting the Sun, the hands of a clock). Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is periodic motion that is to and fro about a fixed mean position (a pendulum, a plucked string). Simple harmonic motion is the simplest oscillatory motion, defined by a restoring force that is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position: F = -k x, where k is the force constant and the minus sign shows the force opposes the displacement.
By Newton's second law, F = m a, so m a = -k x, giving a = -(k/m) x. Writing omega^2 = k/m, we get a = -omega^2 x. Because the acceleration is proportional to displacement and oppositely directed, the motion is SHM. The angular frequency is omega = sqrt(k/m), and the time period is T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi sqrt(m/k). This shows any system with a linear restoring force oscillates simple-harmonically with a frequency set by the ratio of stiffness to inertia.
questions.explanation: Define terms, apply Newton's law to F = -k x, get omega = sqrt(k/m).

questions.question: For a particle in SHM described by x = A sin(omega t + phi), derive expressions for its velocity and acceleration, and describe how displacement, velocity and acceleration vary through one cycle.
questions.answer:
Start with the displacement x = A sin(omega t + phi). Differentiating with respect to time gives the velocity v = dx/dt = A omega cos(omega t + phi). Differentiating again gives the acceleration a = dv/dt = -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x.
Eliminating time, v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
Through one cycle: at the mean position (x = 0) the displacement is zero, the velocity is maximum (A omega) and the acceleration is zero. As the particle moves towards an extreme, x increases, speed falls and the magnitude of acceleration rises. At the extreme (x = A) the displacement is maximum, the velocity is zero and the acceleration is maximum (A omega^2), pointing back towards the mean position. The velocity leads the displacement in phase by pi/2, and the acceleration is exactly out of phase (pi) with the displacement.
questions.explanation: Differentiate twice; discuss phase relations and extreme values.

questions.question: Using the reference circle, show how the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter is simple harmonic. Hence relate the angular frequency to the time period.
questions.answer:
Consider a particle P moving with constant angular speed omega on a circle of radius A (the reference circle). At time t its angular position is (omega t + phi). Drop a perpendicular from P onto a diameter (say the x-axis); call the foot of the perpendicular N. The x-coordinate of N is x = A sin(omega t + phi) [or A cos, depending on the reference axis]. As P goes round the circle, N moves back and forth along the diameter.
The centripetal acceleration of P is A omega^2 directed towards the centre. Its component along the diameter is -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x. Since the acceleration of N is proportional to its displacement and directed towards the centre (mean position), N executes SHM. Thus the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter is SHM with the same amplitude A and angular frequency omega. Because the particle completes one revolution (phase 2 pi) in one period, omega = 2 pi / T, so T = 2 pi / omega and the frequency f = omega / (2 pi).
questions.explanation: Project P onto diameter; component of centripetal acceleration gives -omega^2 x.

questions.question: Derive expressions for the kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy of a particle executing SHM. Show that the total energy is constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude.
questions.answer:
Let a particle of mass m execute SHM x = A sin(omega t + phi) with velocity v = A omega cos(omega t + phi) = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
Kinetic energy KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2).
The restoring force is F = -m omega^2 x, so the potential energy (work done against this force from 0 to x) is PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2.
Total energy E = KE + PE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) + (1/2) m omega^2 x^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.
This is independent of x and t, so the total energy is constant throughout the motion. It is proportional to the square of the amplitude A and to the square of the angular frequency. At the mean position all the energy is kinetic; at the extremes all of it is potential; in between the two forms interchange while their sum stays fixed. If the amplitude is doubled, the total energy becomes four times as large.
questions.explanation: Derive KE and PE, add to get constant (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the time period of a simple pendulum. State the assumptions made and list the factors on which the period depends.
questions.answer:
Consider a bob of mass m on a light inextensible string of length L, displaced through a small angle theta from the vertical. The forces on the bob are its weight mg and the tension T. The tangential component of gravity provides the restoring force: F = -mg sin theta. For small angles (theta less than about 4 degrees), sin theta is approximately theta (in radians), and the displacement along the arc is x = L theta, so theta = x/L. Hence F = -mg (x/L) = -(mg/L) x.
Comparing with F = -k x, the effective force constant is k = mg/L. The motion is therefore SHM with omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(g/L). The time period is T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
Assumptions: the string is light and inextensible, the bob is a point mass, the amplitude is small (so sin theta approx theta), and air resistance is negligible. The period depends only on the length L and on g; it is independent of the mass of the bob and of the amplitude (for small swings).
questions.explanation: Small-angle approximation gives k = mg/L, so T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

questions.question: Derive the time period of a mass m attached to a spring of force constant k. Then explain, with formulae, how connecting two springs in series and in parallel changes the period.
questions.answer:
When a mass m on a spring of constant k is displaced by x, the spring exerts a restoring force F = -k x (Hooke's law). By Newton's second law m a = -k x, so a = -(k/m) x = -omega^2 x with omega = sqrt(k/m). Therefore the motion is SHM with period T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
Parallel combination: if two springs k1 and k2 support the same mass and share the same displacement, their restoring forces add, so the effective constant is k_parallel = k1 + k2. Being stiffer, this gives a smaller period T = 2 pi sqrt(m/(k1 + k2)).
Series combination: if the springs are joined end to end, the same force stretches both and their extensions add, so 1/k_series = 1/k1 + 1/k2, giving k_series = k1 k2/(k1 + k2). This is softer than either spring, so the period T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k_series) is longer. In short, parallel springs shorten the period while series springs lengthen it.
questions.explanation: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); parallel adds k (shorter T), series adds 1/k (longer T).

questions.question: A particle of mass 0.1 kg executes SHM of amplitude 0.05 m and period 0.2 s. Find (a) the angular frequency, (b) the maximum velocity, (c) the maximum acceleration, (d) the total energy, and (e) the velocity at a displacement of 0.03 m.
questions.answer:
Given m = 0.1 kg, A = 0.05 m, T = 0.2 s.
(a) Angular frequency omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 0.2 = 10 pi = 31.4 rad/s.
(b) Maximum velocity v_max = A omega = 0.05 x 31.4 = 1.57 m/s (at the mean position).
(c) Maximum acceleration a_max = A omega^2 = 0.05 x (31.4)^2 = 0.05 x 986 = 49.3 m/s^2 (at the extremes).
(d) Total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = 0.5 x 0.1 x 986 x 0.0025 = 0.123 J.
(e) At x = 0.03 m, v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = 31.4 x sqrt(0.05^2 - 0.03^2) = 31.4 x sqrt(0.0025 - 0.0009) = 31.4 x sqrt(0.0016) = 31.4 x 0.04 = 1.256 m/s.
questions.explanation: omega = 2 pi/T; then apply v_max, a_max, E and v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).

questions.question: Explain free, damped and forced oscillations. Describe resonance, state the condition for it, and give two practical examples (one useful and one to be avoided).
questions.answer:
Free oscillations: when a body is displaced from equilibrium and released, it oscillates at its own natural frequency f0 determined by its inertia and stiffness. In the ideal frictionless case the amplitude stays constant.
Damped oscillations: in reality friction, air resistance or internal losses continuously remove energy, so the amplitude decreases with time and the oscillation eventually dies out. The greater the damping, the faster the decay.
Forced oscillations: if a periodic external force of frequency f is applied, the body is driven to oscillate at the driving frequency f (not its natural frequency). The steady-state amplitude depends on how close f is to f0 and on the damping.
Resonance: when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency (f = f0), energy is transferred most efficiently to the system and the amplitude becomes very large. This is the condition for resonance.
Useful example: tuning a radio, where the circuit is adjusted so its natural frequency matches the desired station's frequency, greatly amplifying that signal. Example to be avoided: marching soldiers break step on a bridge, because if their footfall frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency the resonant amplitude could grow large enough to damage or collapse it.
questions.explanation: Define the three types; resonance at f = f0; radio tuning vs bridge collapse.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A block attached to a horizontal spring is pulled aside and released on a frictionless surface. It is found that its acceleration is always proportional to its displacement from the centre and directed towards the centre, following a = -25 x (SI units).

(i) What type of motion is this?
(ii) What is the angular frequency?
(iii) Find the time period.
(iv) Where is the acceleration zero?
questions.answer:
(i) The motion is simple harmonic motion, because the acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position (a = -omega^2 x).
(ii) Comparing a = -25 x with a = -omega^2 x gives omega^2 = 25, so omega = 5 rad/s.
(iii) T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 5 = 1.26 s.
(iv) The acceleration is zero at the mean (equilibrium) position, x = 0.
questions.explanation: Identify SHM, read omega, compute T, note a = 0 at mean.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The displacement of a particle in SHM is given by x = 0.05 sin(20 t) metre, where t is in seconds.

(i) What are the amplitude and angular frequency?
(ii) Write the expression for velocity.
(iii) Find the maximum velocity.
(iv) Find the maximum acceleration.
questions.answer:
(i) Comparing with x = A sin(omega t): amplitude A = 0.05 m and angular frequency omega = 20 rad/s.
(ii) v = dx/dt = 0.05 x 20 cos(20 t) = 1.0 cos(20 t) m/s.
(iii) Maximum velocity v_max = A omega = 0.05 x 20 = 1.0 m/s (at the mean position).
(iv) Maximum acceleration a_max = A omega^2 = 0.05 x 400 = 20 m/s^2 (at the extremes).
questions.explanation: Read A and omega; differentiate; v_max = A omega, a_max = A omega^2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A particle executing SHM has a speed of 0.16 m/s when it passes through the mean position. Its amplitude of oscillation is 0.04 m.

(i) Find the angular frequency.
(ii) Find the time period.
(iii) Find the speed when the displacement is 0.02 m.
(iv) Find the maximum acceleration.
questions.answer:
(i) At the mean position v = v_max = A omega, so omega = v_max / A = 0.16 / 0.04 = 4 rad/s.
(ii) T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 4 = 1.57 s.
(iii) v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = 4 sqrt(0.04^2 - 0.02^2) = 4 sqrt(0.0016 - 0.0004) = 4 sqrt(0.0012) = 4 x 0.0346 = 0.139 m/s.
(iv) a_max = A omega^2 = 0.04 x 16 = 0.64 m/s^2.
questions.explanation: omega from v_max/A; then T, v(x), a_max.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A tuning fork vibrates and a pendulum swings. A student records that the pendulum completes 15 complete swings in 30 seconds.

(i) What is the time period of the pendulum?
(ii) What is its frequency?
(iii) What is its angular frequency?
(iv) If the phase difference between two such identical pendulums is pi, what does it mean?
questions.answer:
(i) Time period T = total time / number of oscillations = 30 / 15 = 2 s.
(ii) Frequency f = 1/T = 1/2 = 0.5 Hz.
(iii) Angular frequency omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 0.5 = pi = 3.14 rad/s.
(iv) A phase difference of pi means the two pendulums are exactly out of step: when one is at its extreme right the other is at its extreme left, and they always move in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: T = t/N; f = 1/T; omega = 2 pi f; pi phase = opposite.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A particle of mass 0.1 kg executes SHM with amplitude 0.2 m and angular frequency 5 rad/s.

(i) Find the total energy.
(ii) Find the kinetic energy at the mean position.
(iii) Find the potential energy at the extreme position.
(iv) At what displacement are KE and PE equal?
questions.answer:
(i) Total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = 0.5 x 0.1 x 25 x 0.04 = 0.05 J.
(ii) At the mean position all the energy is kinetic, so KE = 0.05 J.
(iii) At the extreme position all the energy is potential, so PE = 0.05 J.
(iv) KE = PE at x = A/sqrt(2) = 0.2 / 1.414 = 0.141 m, where each equals 0.025 J.
questions.explanation: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2; KE max at mean, PE max at extreme; equal at A/sqrt(2).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In SHM the kinetic energy is KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) and the potential energy is PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2.

(i) Where is KE maximum and where is PE maximum?
(ii) What is the ratio KE : PE at x = A/2?
(iii) Show that the total energy is independent of x.
(iv) If amplitude is halved, how does the total energy change?
questions.answer:
(i) KE is maximum at the mean position (x = 0); PE is maximum at the extremes (x = A).
(ii) At x = A/2: KE proportional to (A^2 - A^2/4) = 3A^2/4; PE proportional to A^2/4. So KE : PE = 3 : 1.
(iii) E = KE + PE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) + (1/2) m omega^2 x^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, which contains no x, so it is constant.
(iv) E is proportional to A^2. If A is halved, E becomes one quarter of its original value.
questions.explanation: KE max at mean; ratio 3:1 at A/2; sum constant; E prop A^2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A simple pendulum of length 1.0 m oscillates at a place where g = 9.8 m/s^2.

(i) Write the formula for the period of a simple pendulum.
(ii) Calculate the period.
(iii) What would happen to the period if the length were made four times?
(iv) Does the period depend on the mass of the bob?
questions.answer:
(i) T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
(ii) T = 2 pi sqrt(1.0/9.8) = 2 pi sqrt(0.102) = 2 pi x 0.319 = 2.0 s.
(iii) Since T is proportional to sqrt(L), making L four times increases T by a factor of 2, giving 4.0 s.
(iv) No. The period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) contains no mass term, so it is independent of the mass of the bob.
questions.explanation: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2.0 s; 4L doubles T; mass independent.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A mass of 0.25 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 100 N/m and set into vertical oscillation.

(i) Write the formula for the period of a loaded spring.
(ii) Calculate the angular frequency.
(iii) Calculate the time period.
(iv) Calculate the frequency.
questions.answer:
(i) T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
(ii) omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(100/0.25) = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s.
(iii) T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 20 = 0.314 s.
(iv) f = 1/T = 1/0.314 = 3.18 Hz.
questions.explanation: omega = sqrt(k/m); T = 2 pi/omega; f = 1/T.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two springs, each of force constant 200 N/m, can be connected to a 0.5 kg block either in series or in parallel.

(i) Find the effective constant for the parallel combination.
(ii) Find the effective constant for the series combination.
(iii) Find the angular frequency for the parallel case.
(iv) Which arrangement gives the shorter period, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Parallel: k_parallel = 200 + 200 = 400 N/m.
(ii) Series: 1/k = 1/200 + 1/200 = 2/200, so k_series = 100 N/m.
(iii) Parallel omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(400/0.5) = sqrt(800) = 28.3 rad/s.
(iv) The parallel arrangement gives the shorter period, because it is stiffer (larger k) and T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) decreases as k increases.
questions.explanation: Parallel 400, series 100; omega = 28.3; parallel shorter T.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When a child on a swing is pushed gently at the right moments, the swing goes higher and higher. In another situation, a bridge can sway dangerously when many people walk across it in step.

(i) Name the phenomenon common to both situations.
(ii) State the condition required for it.
(iii) Why is the swing an example of forced oscillation?
(iv) Why do soldiers break step while crossing a bridge?
questions.answer:
(i) The common phenomenon is resonance.
(ii) Resonance requires the frequency of the external (driving) force to equal the natural frequency of the oscillating system.
(iii) The swing is a forced oscillation because it is kept going by a periodic external push; when that push is timed to the swing's natural frequency, resonance builds up a large amplitude.
(iv) Soldiers break step so that their marching frequency does not match the bridge's natural frequency; if it did, resonance could build up a large, possibly destructive, amplitude in the bridge.
questions.explanation: Resonance; driving frequency = natural frequency; swing driven; break step avoids resonance.
